We used a brush to extract a single larva from the sucrose solution and rinse it in water to remove residual sucrose. We then placed the single larva in the centre of the agarose plate and shut the tracker door tightly. Prior to starting all experiment runs, we gave larvae a short period of time to acclimate to their new environment and, in the case of high-throughput experiments, disperse so they were not touching each other.

### Verification of optogenetic and thermogenetic stimulation efficiency

#### Experiment procedures

We assessed the multi-larva tracker’s optogenetic and thermogenetic stimulation efficiency through open-loop proof-of-principle experiments. The 1 min experiment protocol began with a 15 s initialisation period in which larvae acclimated to the agarose plate and behaviour classifiers stabilised. In three subsequent 15 s stimulation rounds, larvae received 5 s of open-loop stimulation followed by 10 s without stimulation (Figure 2C). Optogenetics were performed with a combined red light intensity of 285 µW/cm2 from two DMDs as described above. Thermogenetics were performed with the 1490 nm laser at 40% of its maximum available 5.26 W intensity.

#### Data analysis

Analysis of these open-loop optogenetic and thermogenetic experiment data (Figure 2D, Figure 2E) was conducted using custom MATLAB software. After equally splitting each 60 s experiment into either 0.5 s or 5 s time bins, we retained objects for analysis that fulfilled strict criteria: (i) for all bins following the 15 s initialisation period, the object’s initial detection must have occurred at least 15s prior to the start of the bin; (ii) the object must have been detected in every frame of the bin (i. e. it retained its identity and did not collide with another object); and (iii) the mean of the smoothed centroid velocity across the object’s detection period in the bin was at least 0.5 mm/s. For each larva, the criterion for rolling, crawling, or bending was detection of the corresponding behaviour at least once during a given bin, irrespective of the behaviour’s duration. The number of larvae performing each behaviour in a given bin was then divided by the total number of larvae in the bin to give the fractions displayed in Figure 2D and Figure 2E.

### Temporal dynamics of larval heating

#### Experiment procedures and data analysis

To quantify the time course of larval heating with our setup (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), we performed additional open-loop stimulation experiments with the 1470 nm laser. The experiment protocol began with a 30 s initialisation period without heat stimulation. Then the IR laser was turned on at 50% intensity for 20 s. During this stimulation period, the heat camera was used to maintain an intended temperature of 30℃at each larval location, as described above. Ten runs of this experiment were performed, with four larvae placed on the agarose plate per run. To analyse these data, recorded temperatures at each larval location for every point in time were collected.

### High-throughput classical conditioning

#### Experiment procedures

Eight larvae were trained during each run of the classical conditioning experiment, with 18 runs for experimental larvae and 14 runs for control larvae. Training began after an initial 30 s initialisation period. Forward-paired training consisted of eight replicate training rounds, yielding a total training period lasting 840 s. Each round began with 20 s of red light illumination (via two 613nm DMDs with combined intensity of 550 µW/cm2, as described above), followed by 5 s without stimulation and then 20 s of IR illumination (via 1470 nm laser). This IR illumination caused larval heating up to 27.5℃, which was maintained using the closed-loop temperature control system described above. Each round ended with 60 s without stimulation. Backward-paired training was identical to forward-paired with the exception that IR illumination occurred first, followed by red light illumination. 60 s without stimulation followed the training period. In the subsequent testing period, larvae were illuminated for 20 s with the same wavelength and intensity of red light as during training. The testing period involve three rounds of this illumination, with 45 s of no stimulation between each replicate (Figure 3A).

#### Data analysis

For this analysis, we divided each testing round into three time windows: PRE (10–0 s before light onset), ON (0–20 s after light onset), and OFF (0–20 s after light offset). Only larvae that were tracked for all three ON and OFF windows during the testing period were analysed. To account for violated normality and sphericity assumptions, we calculated the difference in percentage bending values between the ON and OFF windows (i. e. ON-OFF) for each individual larva. These percentage bending differences were then compared between training protocols and genotypes to study the effects of training on larval bending behavior during the testing period. Because percentage bending differences were not normally distributed, we used two-sided Mann–Whitney U tests to assess how bending behaviour differed between training protocols and genotypes.

### High-throughput operant conditioning

#### Experiment procedures

Each run of the operant conditioning experiment protocol (Figure 4B) consisted of 10–12 larvae on the plate. The protocol began and ended with a 1 min test period without optogenetic stimulation. Between these test periods were four, 3 min training rounds during which larvae received red light stimulation of 285 µW/cm2 (combined from two DMDs as described above) for the entire duration of the detected bend. Which side received stimulation was randomised across trials such that approximately 50% of larvae were trained to develop a right bend preference and 50%a left bend preference. No stimulus was triggered when the larva was bending right or when its body was straight. The test periods were each separated by 3 min periods without stimulation. After the first minute of this period, a brush was used to gently move all larvae back to the centre of the plate and larvae were given time to recover before the beginning of the next training round. This recentring addresses problems encountered when performing prolonged experiments with freely behaving larvae on a small agarose plate. The longer larvae are left undisturbed, the more likely they are to touch the plate’s edge, causing tracking disruption and temporary loss of valid objects. This shrinks sample size and reduces training efficiency by decreasing the proportion of animals receiving the stimulus.

Control experiments were designed so that valid objects received optogenetic stimulation uncorrelated with behaviour. These control experiments were split into 60 s time bins, during which each valid object was randomly assigned a stimulus train from this same time bin, pulled from a prior experiment where stimulation correlated with behaviour.

#### Data analysis

Data analysis was conducted using custom MATLAB software. After equally splitting each experiment into 60 s time bins, we retained objects for analysis that fulfilled strict criteria: (i) the object must have been detected in every frame of the bin (i.e. it retained its identity and did not collide with another object); (ii) the object’s initial detection must have occurred at least 20 s prior to the start of the bin; (iii) at no point during the bin did the smoothed velocity of the larval centroid exceed 1.5 mm/s; and (iv) the mean of the smoothed centroid velocity across the object’s detection period in the bin was at least 0.5 mm/s.

To analyse operant conditioning of bend direction preference, it was necessary to further smooth the raw time series of left and right bends post-acquisition: two bends to the same side separated by less than 200ms were combined into a single long bend, and short bends of less than 200ms were removed from analysis. We then counted, for each larva, the numbers of left and right bends initiated within each 60 s time bin. This was defined as the bend rate towards the respective direction. Within each bin, the difference in bend rate was defined, for each larva, as the number of bends towards the side paired with the optogenetic stimulus minus the number of bends towards the unstimulated side. We pooled together all larval data within each bin because bends to the left and right were each paired with the optogenetic stimulus for approximately half of the larvae. For the control condition in which larvae received random stimulation during 50% of bends regardless of direction, bend rates were calculated to the left and right and the difference in bend rate was calculated between left and right. Bend rates to either side were compared to each other using a two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test. This statistical choice was driven by the known pairing of these spatial observations for individual larvae and the non-normality exhibited across distributions of differences between these paired bend rates. Similar reasoning guided the usage of a two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test to compare the difference in bend rate to 0. The behaviour characteristics of experimental animals were compared to each control group using a two-sided Mann-Whitney U test.

### Low-throughput operant conditioning

#### Experiment procedures

Each run of the operant conditioning experiment protocol (Figure 4—figure supplement 3) consisted of one larva on the plate. The protocol began and ended with a 1 min test period without optogenetic stimulation. Between these test periods were two, 3 min training rounds during which larvae received red light stimulation of 385 µW/cm2 for the entire duration of the detected bend. Which side received stimulation was randomised across trials such that approximately 50% of larvae were trained to develop a right bend preference and 50%a left bend preference. No stimulus was triggered when the larva was bending right or when its body was straight. The two test periods were separated by a 3-min period without stimulation.

#### Data analysis

Data analysis was conducted using custom MATLAB software. Each experiment was equally split into 60 s time bins. We then counted, for each larva, the numbers of left and right bends initiated within each 60 s bin. This was defined as the bend rate towards the respective direction. Within each bin, the difference in bend rate was defined, for each larva, as the number of bends towards the side paired with the optogenetic stimulus minus the number of bends towards the unstimulated side. We pooled together all larval data within each bin because bends to the left and right were each paired with the optogenetic stimulus for approximately half of the larvae.

### Immunohistochemistry and confocal imaging

All dissections, immunohistochemical stainings, and confocal imaging were done using a procedure adapted from Jenett et al., 2012 and Li et al., 2014. Larval CNSs were dissected in cold 1x phosphate buffer saline (PBS, Corning Cellgro, #21–040) and transferred to tubes filled with cold 4% paraformaldehyde (Electron Microscopy Sciences, #15,713S) in 1x PBS. Tubes were incubated for 1 hr at room temperature. The tissue was then washed four times in 1x PBS with 1% Triton X-100 (#X100, Sigma Aldrich St. Louis, Missouri) (PBT) and incubated in 1:20 donkey serum (#017-000-121, Jackson Immuno Research, West Grove, Pennsylvania) in PBT for 2 hr at room temperature.

The tissue was then incubated in the primary antibody solution, first for 4 hr at room temperature and then for two nights at 4℃. This solution contained mouse anti-Neuroglian (1:50, #BP104 anti-Neuroglian, Developmental Studies Hybridoma Bank, Iowa City, Iowa), rabbit anti-GFP (1:500, #A11122, Life Technologies, Waltham, Massachusetts) and rat anti-N-Cadherin (1:50, #DN-Ex #8, Developmental Studies Hybridoma Bank, Iowa City, Iowa) in PBT. This solution was then removed and the tissue washed four times in PBT. The tissue was then incubated in the secondary antibody solution, first for 4 hr at room temperature and then for two nights at 4℃. This solution contained Alexa Fluor 568 donkey anti-mouse (1:500, #A10037, Invitrogen, Waltham, Massachusetts), FITC donkey anti-rabbit (1:500, #711-095-152, Jackson Immuno Research West Grove, Pennsylvania) and Alexa Fluor 647 donkey anti-rat (1:500, #712-605-153, Jackson Immuno Research West Grove, Pennsylvania) in PBT. After removal of the secondary solution, the tissue was washed in PBT four times and mounted on a coverslip coated with poly-L-lysine (#P1524-25MG, Sigma Aldrich, St. Louis, Missouri).

The coverslip with the CNSs was dehydrated by moving it through a series of jars containing ethanol at increasing concentrations (30%, 50%, 75%, 95%, 100%, 100%, 100%) for 10 min each. The tissue was then cleared by soaking the coverslip with xylene (#X5-500, Fisher Scientific, Waltham, Massachusetts) three times for 5 min each. Finally, the coverslips were mounted in dibutyl phthalate in xylene (DPX, #13512, Electron Microscopy Sciences, Hatfield, Pennsylvania) with the tissue facing down on a microscope slide with spacers. The DPX was allowed to dry for at least two nights prior to confocal imaging with an LSM 710 microscope (Zeiss).

Details on the confocal imaging settings are provided in the respective figure captions. Confocal images were analysed using Fiji (ImageJ). Neurons were counted by specifying regions of interest around the cell bodies using raw image stacks.

Essential revisions:

1) Because the optogenetically induced operant learning has a modest effect, the Reviewers would like to see replication of operant conditioning using the thermogenetic paradigm (shown to be effective in Figure 2).

2) More rigorous analyses of the phenotype (e.g., showing pre and postbending behaviors, see Reviewer #1… additional statistical tests, see Reviewer #2… additional controls, see Reviewer #3).

3) All reviewers were concerned about the artificial nature of the US. If operant conditioning can be evoked with nociceptive pain, that would be great. If not, a more careful discussion of the limitations of using artificial stimuli in the interpretation and discussion would suffice.

Reviewer #1 (Recommendations for the authors):

Below I will list the criticism summarized in the previous section

1) To validate the set up the authors induce rolling behavior by thermo- or optogenetically activating two sets of previously described neurons in individual larva. Both approaches show convincing induction of the behavior per se. However, there seems to be an interaction of the different tools used (thermo and opto-genetic) and the targeted neurons: the authors observe different dynamics of the behavior across the three stimulation cycles depending on stimulation method and labeled neurons. These findings make it difficult to understand why the authors choose only the optogenetic activation to investigate operant conditioning. Thus, the authors should repeat key experiments using thermogenetic tools (see below).

2) The strength of the setup is that individual animals can be targeted. Though the presented data show that behavior can be reliably induced in stimulated animals, it lacks the information about the behavior of non-targeted larva during the stimulation. Thus, it would strengthen the work if the authors could show the behavior of the non-targeted larva during the time when targeted larva receive light or heat.

3) The origin of the relative difference between left and right bending in the paired group is not entirely clear. Thus, it will be important to strengthen the work by additional experiments investigating temporal relationship between the CS and US. Ideally the experiments should focus on understanding why the training results in a reduction of the unreinforced behavior.

4) The authors should consider that given the small effects, it has to be ensured that the observed differences originate from training and are not mere pre-training biases. Though they show the pretraining results for one of the experiments (Figure 3b, the trained group), the pretraining bending is very relevant for each of the operant learning experiments. In fact, training induced effects should not only be measured by looking at the left vs right bending in the final test but as a change between pre versus post or between a trained and a mock control group. This is done for one group (Ddc-GAL4) in Figure 3b but will be mandatory for all operant learning experiments.

5) It would improve the accessibility of the learning induced change of behavior if the authors could show the pre vs post training results for each run (10-12 larva in a plate). Further, they should plot the numbers of reinforced behaviors in each of the training protocols and relate it to the test performance.

6) The presented data clearly suggests a decrease of the unstimulated bending rather than a change in the reinforced behavior. Though the authors mention it, they do not explain or discuss it. It will be very important for the logic of the manuscript that the authors explain this phenomenon and how it relates to operant conditioning (see point 3).

7) Though the manuscript discusses most of the data carefully, in my view the authors miss an important issue: it remains to be shown if fly larva are capable of operant learning using external reward or punishment. The presented evidence is based on artificial activation of neurons, which arguably is a hint but not a prove that operant conditioning is withing the repertoire of a fly larva, an issue the authors should mention and discuss.

claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: Bending differences following backward-paired training did not differ significantly between genotypes.

claims.claim: These results provide the first evidence that larvae can perform classical conditioning with significant offset-to-onset gaps (9 s) between stimuli.

claims.evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the finding based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claims.claim: Biogenic amine neurotransmitters including dopamine, octopamine, and serotonin can provide reinforcement signals across the animal kingdom.
claims.source: Across the animal kingdom, biogenic amine neurotransmitters including dopamine, octopamine, and serotonin can provide reinforcement signals (Giurfa, 2006; Hawkins and Byrne, 2015; Meneses and Liy-Salmeron, 2012; Fee and Goldberg, 2011).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: The Ddc-Gal4 driver covers a broad set of neurons containing dopamine and serotonin.
claims.source: The Ddc-Gal4 driver is ideally suited for this purpose, covering a broad set of neurons containing these biogenic amines (Li et al., 2000; Sitaraman et al., 2008; Lundell and Hirsh, 1994), including the MB-innervating protocerebral anterior medial (PAM) cluster dopaminergic neurons (Liu et al., 2012; Aso et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about the expression pattern of this driver, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Ddc-Gal4 includes the MB-innervating protocerebral anterior medial (PAM) cluster dopaminergic neurons.
claims.source: The Ddc-Gal4 driver is ideally suited for this purpose, covering a broad set of neurons containing these biogenic amines (Li et al., 2000; Sitaraman et al., 2008; Lundell and Hirsh, 1994), including the MB-innervating protocerebral anterior medial (PAM) cluster dopaminergic neurons (Liu et al., 2012; Aso et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: PAM cluster activation serves as both a necessary and sufficient reward signal in classical conditioning.
claims.source: Although the function of most Ddc neurons is unknown, PAM cluster activation serves as both a necessary and sufficient reward signal in classical conditioning (Rohwedder et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2012; Vogt et al., 2014; Cognigni et al., 2018; Waddell, 2013), and collective activation of Ddc neurons can substitute for an olfactory conditioning reward in adult flies (Liu et al., 2012; Shyu et al., 2017; Aso et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Collective activation of Ddc neurons can substitute for an olfactory conditioning reward in adult flies.
claims.source: Although the function of most Ddc neurons is unknown, PAM cluster activation serves as both a necessary and sufficient reward signal in classical conditioning (Rohwedder et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2012; Vogt et al., 2014; Cognigni et al., 2018; Waddell, 2013), and collective activation of Ddc neurons can substitute for an olfactory conditioning reward in adult flies (Liu et al., 2012; Shyu et al., 2017; Aso et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: The average duration of a larval bend is 1.35 s (sd = 1.67 s, n = 4622 bends).
claims.source: Knowing that the average duration of a larval bend is only a third of that time (mean = 1.35 s, sd = 1.67 s, n = 4622 bends), we concluded that closed-loop heat stimulation would activate neurons of interest only after a noticeable delay relative to behaviour detection, with possibly other behaviours occurring during the delay period.
claims.evidence: This is a measurement from behavioral data.

claims.claim: Closed-loop heat stimulation would activate neurons of interest only after a noticeable delay relative to behaviour detection.
claims.source: Knowing that the average duration of a larval bend is only a third of that time (mean = 1.35 s, sd = 1.67 s, n = 4622 bends), we concluded that closed-loop heat stimulation would activate neurons of interest only after a noticeable delay relative to behaviour detection, with possibly other behaviours occurring during the delay period.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of heating time and bend duration.

claims.claim: Quicker heating was achievable with increased laser intensity, but risked overshooting the desired temperature and damaging larval tissue.

claims.evidence: This describes an experimental observation about the limitations of the heating system.

claims.claim: Any safe thermogenetic approach would be too slow to temporally align the US induced via larval heating with a specific larval action.
claims.source: Any safe thermogenetic approach would therefore be too slow to temporally align the US induced via larval heating with a specific larval action.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion about the limitations of thermogenetic approaches for operant conditioning.

claims.claim: Mild heat is more aversive to larvae than visible red light.
claims.source: With mild heat more aversive to larvae than visible red light (compare bending in control larvae in Figure 2D, E, ), we favoured optogenetics over thermogenetics for our operant conditioning paradigm.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of control data in Figures 2D and 2E.

claims.claim: The time between the tracker detecting a left bend and light onset was no longer than 50 ms.
claims.source: The time between the tracker detecting a left bend and light onset was no longer than 50 ms.
claims.evidence: This is a technical specification of the system's temporal precision.

claims.claim: Larvae were recentered between training rounds to mitigate the experimental side effects of larvae reaching the plate's edge.
claims.source: We performed this recentring to mitigate the experimental side effects of larvae reaching the plate's edge (see Materials and methods for more details).
claims.evidence: This describes an experimental procedure and its rationale.

claims.claim: In the 1 min test before the first training round, Ddc>CsChrimson larvae showed no significant difference in bend rate to either side.
claims.source: In the 1 min test before the first training round, we observed no significant difference in bend rate to either side for Ddc>CsChrimson larvae (p>0.5; Figure 4C).

claims.claim: Larval bend rate to the stimulated side was significantly greater than that of the unstimulated side throughout the majority of training for Ddc>CsChrimson larvae.

claims.evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Ddc activation can function as a rewarding stimulus that larvae increasingly seek with time.
claims.source: These findings suggest that Ddc activation can function as a rewarding stimulus that larvae increasingly seek with time.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the training data.

claims.claim: In the 1 min test after the fourth training round, Ddc>CsChrimson larvae showed a significantly greater bend rate towards the side paired with red light stimulation during training compared to the previously unstimulated side.
claims.source: In the 1 min test after the fourth training round, larvae showed a significantly greater bend rate towards the side paired with red light stimulation during training (mean = 4.84, sd = 2.40, n = 143) compared to the previously unstimulated side (mean = 4.10, sd = 2.23, n = 143) (p=0.0007, CLES = 0.59; Figure 4C) indicating operant conditioning of bend direction.
claims.evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 4C, demonstrating operant conditioning.

claims.claim: Fictive Ddc activation with the single-larva tracker yielded a significant bend direction preference to the previously stimulated versus previously unstimulated side after training.
claims.source: Fictive Ddc activation with this system also yielded a significant bend direction preference to the previously stimulated (mean = 5.77, sd = 2.71, n = 109) versus previously unstimulated (mean = 4.73, sd = 2.73, n = 109) side (p=0.0043, CLES = 0.63), after training.
claims.evidence: This is an experimental result from the single-larva tracker shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: Effector control larvae (UAS-CsChrimson without Ddc-GAL4) show no difference in bend rate to either side after training.

claims.evidence: This is an experimental result from control larvae shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: Potential leaky expression of CsChrimson in neurons outside of the Ddc expression pattern is not causing operant learning.
claims.source: Based on these control larvae, we concluded that potential leaky expression of CsChrimson in neurons outside of the Ddc expression pattern is not causing operant learning (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the control experiment results.

claims.claim: Larvae that received random, uncorrelated stimulation during 50% of all bends showed no difference in absolute left and right bend rates before, during and after training (with one exception).

claims.evidence: This is a statistical comparison shown in Figure 4H.

claims.claim: After training, bend rates for larvae that received uncorrelated training were indistinguishable from the rate of pair-trained larvae bending to the previously stimulated side.
claims.source: Further dissection of bend rates to each side showed that, after training, bend rates averaged together for larvae that received uncorrelated training (mean = 4.80, sd = 2.39, n = 160) were indistinguishable from the rate of pair-trained larvae bending to the previously stimulated side (mean = 4.84, sd = 2.40, n = 143) (p>0.5; Figure 4G).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical comparison shown in Figure 4G.

claims.claim: Larvae that received uncorrelated training showed a significantly higher bend rate compared to pair-trained larvae bending to the previously unstimulated side.

claims.evidence: This is a statistical comparison shown in Figure 4G.

claims.claim: Pair-trained Ddc>CsChrimson larvae have learnt to avoid the unstimulated side.
claims.source: This suggests that the pair-trained Ddc>CsChrimson larvae have learnt to avoid the unstimulated side.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison with uncorrelated training controls.

claims.claim: There is growing evidence from classical conditioning that larvae can learn that an unpaired stimulus predicts the absence of reinforcement.
claims.source: There is growing evidence from classical conditioning that larvae can learn that an unpaired stimulus predicts the absence of reinforcement (Schleyer et al., 2018; Eschbach et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Larvae may be forming memories of opposite valence in the operant conditioning paradigm, bending less to the unstimulated side because bending to that side predicts the absence of appetitive Ddc activation.

claims.evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism underlying the observed behavior.

claims.claim: Some prior work in adult flies suggests that the MB is involved in operant conditioning.
claims.source: Some prior work in adult flies suggests that the MB is involved in operant conditioning (Sun et al., 2020), while other studies in the adult suggest that operant conditioning does not require the MB (Booker and Quinn, 1981; Wolf et al., 1998; Colomb and Brembs, 2010; Colomb and Brembs, 2016) and may instead involve motor neuron plasticity (Colomb and Brembs, 2016).
claims.evidence: This summarizes conflicting findings in the literature, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Other studies in adult flies suggest that operant conditioning does not require the MB and may instead involve motor neuron plasticity.
claims.source: Some prior work in adult flies suggests that the MB is involved in operant conditioning (Sun et al., 2020), while other studies in the adult suggest that operant conditioning does not require the MB (Booker and Quinn, 1981; Wolf et al., 1998; Colomb and Brembs, 2010; Colomb and Brembs, 2016) and may instead involve motor neuron plasticity (Colomb and Brembs, 2016).
claims.evidence: This summarizes findings in the literature, supported by citations.

claims.claim: In classical conditioning of both adult and larval Drosophila, the MB has been identified as a convergence site for the external CS and the rewarding or punishing US.
claims.source: In classical conditioning of both adult and larval Drosophila, the MB has been identified as a convergence site for the external CS and the rewarding or punishing US (Cognigni et al., 2018; Heisenberg et al., 1985; Heisenberg, 2003; Rohwedder et al., 2016; Vogt et al., 2014; Saumweber et al., 2018; Owald and Waddell, 2015).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: In each larval brain hemisphere, the MB comprises approximately 110 CS-encoding Kenyon cells (KCs).
claims.source: In each larval brain hemisphere, the MB comprises approximately 110 CS-encoding Kenyon cells (KCs) (Aso et al., 2014; Honegger et al., 2011; Berck et al., 2016; Lin et al., 2014; Owald and Waddell, 2015; Campbell et al., 2013; Turner et al., 2008; Eichler et al., 2017) that synapse onto 24 MB output neurons (MBONs) driving approach or avoidance (Aso et al., 2014; Owald and Waddell, 2015; Perisse et al., 2016; Séjourné et al., 2011; Saumweber et al., 2018; Shyu et al., 2017; Plaçais et al., 2013; Eichler et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about MB anatomy, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Kenyon cells synapse onto 24 MB output neurons (MBONs) driving approach or avoidance.
claims.source: In each larval brain hemisphere, the MB comprises approximately 110 CS-encoding Kenyon cells (KCs) (Aso et al., 2014; Honegger et al., 2011; Berck et al., 2016; Lin et al., 2014; Owald and Waddell, 2015; Campbell et al., 2013; Turner et al., 2008; Eichler et al., 2017) that synapse onto 24 MB output neurons (MBONs) driving approach or avoidance (Aso et al., 2014; Owald and Waddell, 2015; Perisse et al., 2016; Séjourné et al., 2011; Saumweber et al., 2018; Shyu et al., 2017; Plaçais et al., 2013; Eichler et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about MB connectivity, supported by citations.

claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about MB plasticity mechanisms, supported by citations.

claims.claim: In vertebrates, dopamine release is crucial for not only learning but also action selection.
claims.source: In vertebrates, dopamine release is crucial for not only learning but also action selection (Grillner et al., 2013).

claims.claim: Targeted activation of only brain and SEZ dopaminergic neurons may affect the larval motor program in a functionally analogous manner to vertebrate dopamine's role in action selection.

claims.evidence: This is a statistical comparison shown in Figure 4H.

claims.claim: The dopaminergic and serotonergic neurons in the brain are not sufficient for operant conditioning.
claims.source: Based on these results, the dopaminergic and serotonergic neurons in the brain are not sufficient for operant conditioning.

results.result: The authors developed a high-throughput multi-larva tracking system that performs real-time behavior detection of up to 16 larvae simultaneously with independent optogenetic and thermogenetic stimulation delivered with high temporal precision (≤50ms for optogenetics, 4s heating time for thermogenetics) in both open- and closed-loop configurations.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C63 and C122 provide comprehensive technical specifications with measured performance metrics. The system architecture is well-documented with hardware specifications, timing measurements (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), and behavior detection performance values provided in methods. The 4s heating time and ≤50ms optogenetic delay are experimentally measured values.

results.result: Proof-of-principle optogenetic experiments demonstrate that combined red light from two DMDs successfully activates CsChrimson-expressing neurons, triggering rolling behavior in >50% of 69F06>CsChrimson and >90% of 72F11>CsChrimson larvae during 5s stimulation, with significantly elevated bending compared to attP2>CsChrimson controls, while red light alone is minimally aversive.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C80 present optogenetic validation data with appropriate controls (Figure 2D). Statistical comparisons use Fisher's exact test with Bonferroni correction across multiple time bins. The low bending in controls (C77) supports the inference that red light is minimally aversive. Sample sizes are adequate (n=32-46 per group).

results.result: Thermogenetic stimulation with 1490nm IR laser activates dTrpA1-expressing neurons, triggering rolling in >60% of 69F06>dTrpA1 and >40% of 72F11>dTrpA1 larvae with a predictable 4-5s temporal delay, though control larvae show elevated bending indicative of mild heat aversion.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C89 demonstrate thermogenetic efficacy with measured temporal dynamics (Figure 2E). The 4-5s delay is consistent with heating kinetics (Figure 2—figure supplement 1). The caveat about heat aversion in controls (C88-C89) is appropriately acknowledged and limits the utility of thermogenetics for certain paradigms. Statistical tests are appropriate.

results.result: Drosophila larvae demonstrate trace conditioning for the first time, showing reduced attraction to Or42b activation after forward-paired training with Basin neuron activation (9s gap between CS offset and US onset). Experimental larvae showed significantly smaller percentage bending differences after forward-paired training (mean=-5.22%) compared to backward-paired training (mean=-29.65%, p<0.0001, CLES=0.852), and compared to control larvae receiving heat alone (mean=-21.76%, p<0.0001, CLES=0.752).
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C111 and C177-C181 present the first demonstration of trace conditioning in larvae with appropriate experimental design (Figure 3). The 9s gap calculation (C97) accounts for measured heating dynamics. Statistical analyses use Mann-Whitney U tests appropriate for non-normal distributions. Multiple controls (backward-paired, genetic controls) strengthen conclusions. However, the novelty claim (C7, C111) relies on authors' literature knowledge and should be independently verified.

results.result: Control larvae without dTrpA1 in Basin neurons also showed reduced attraction after forward-paired training (mean=-21.76%) compared to backward-paired (mean=-30.22%, p=0.009, CLES=0.648), suggesting mild heat alone can weaken attraction to Or42b, consistent with prior work using heat as reinforcement.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C106 appropriately identify a control effect that complicates interpretation. The statistical comparison is valid, and the connection to prior work (Khurana et al., 2012) is appropriate. This control result is important for understanding the contribution of Basin activation versus heat alone, and the authors correctly note the significantly larger effect in experimental larvae (C107-C108).

results.result: Drosophila larvae demonstrate operant conditioning of bend direction through optogenetic activation of Ddc neurons. After training, Ddc>CsChrimson larvae showed significantly greater bend rate to the previously stimulated side (mean=4.84) versus unstimulated side (mean=4.10, p=0.0007, CLES=0.59), with no initial bias before training (p>0.5).
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C9 and C124-C127 present operant conditioning results with appropriate experimental design (Figure 4). Statistical tests (Wilcoxon signed-rank) are appropriate for paired data. The lack of initial bias (C124) and development of preference during training (C125-C126) support operant learning interpretation. Sample size (n=143) is adequate. Replication on single-larva tracker (C128) strengthens the finding.

results.result: The operant conditioning result was replicated on a single-larva tracker, showing significant bend direction preference (p=0.0043, CLES=0.63), while effector control larvae (UAS-CsChrimson without Ddc-GAL4) showed no preference, confirming absence of leaky expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C128-C130 provide important replication on an independent system and genetic control. The effector control is critical for ruling out leaky expression artifacts. Statistical test is appropriate and sample size adequate (n=109).

results.result: Larvae receiving random, uncorrelated stimulation during 50% of bends showed no directional bias and significantly lower difference in bend rates after training (mean=-0.28) compared to pair-trained larvae (mean=0.74, p=0.0020, CLES=0.60). Uncorrelated-trained larvae bent significantly more than pair-trained larvae to the unstimulated side (p=0.0037), suggesting pair-trained larvae learned to avoid the unstimulated side.
results.evaluation: Claims C131-C135 present critical control experiments demonstrating that learning requires contingency between behavior and stimulation. Statistical comparisons are appropriate. The interpretation about learning to avoid the unstimulated side (C135) is reasonable given the data pattern, though alternative explanations exist.

results.result: Restricting Ddc expression to brain and SEZ (using tsh-Gal80) eliminated operant conditioning. Ddc>CsChrimson, tsh>Gal80 larvae showed no learned direction preference after training (p>0.5) and significantly lower difference in bend rate (mean=0.029) compared to Ddc>CsChrimson larvae (mean=0.74, p=0.012, CLES=0.58), indicating VNC dopaminergic and serotonergic neurons are critical for operant conditioning.
results.evaluation: Claims C146-C153 use intersectional genetics to dissect circuit requirements. The tsh-Gal80 expression pattern is validated by immunohistochemistry (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, C145). Statistical comparisons are appropriate. The conclusion that VNC neurons are critical (C153) is well-supported, though the inference that brain neurons are 'not sufficient' (C152) is more cautious than claiming they are unnecessary.

results.result: Activating PAM cluster dopaminergic neurons (58E02>CsChrimson) did not induce operant conditioning. Larvae showed no learned direction preference after training (p>0.5) and significantly lower difference in bend rate (mean=-0.14) compared to Ddc>CsChrimson larvae (mean=0.74, p=0.015, CLES=0.58), supporting the idea that operant conditioning may not be mediated by the mushroom body.
results.evaluation: Claims C155-C163 test MB involvement using PAM-specific driver. Negative result is appropriately interpreted with caution (C163). The observation of preference to unstimulated side during training (C156) raises questions about motor control effects that are appropriately acknowledged. Sample size adequate (n=145). This result contrasts with classical conditioning where MB is critical.

results.result: Activating dopaminergic TH neurons (excluding PAM cluster) did not yield significant learned direction preference in operant conditioning, with no difference in bend rates before or after training (p>0.5).
results.evaluation: Claims C165 and C189 present negative result with TH-Gal4 driver. Statistical test appropriate and sample sizes adequate (n=75 before, n=122 after). The negative result is important for circuit dissection but must be interpreted cautiously as absence of evidence.

results.result: Activating serotonergic Tph neurons was sufficient to induce operant conditioning, with significantly higher bend rate to stimulated side (mean=3.62) versus unstimulated side (mean=3.29) after training (p=0.019, CLES=0.58). However, direct comparison between TH and Tph groups was not significant (p>0.5), suggesting cautious interpretation that Tph neurons are sufficient but TH neurons may weakly contribute.
results.evaluation: Claims C167-C171 and C190-C191 demonstrate sufficiency of serotonergic neurons with appropriate statistical tests. The cautious interpretation (C170-C171) acknowledging that lack of significance between TH and Tph doesn't prove equivalence is scientifically appropriate. Sample sizes adequate (n=77 before, n=126 after for Tph).

results.result: Restricting Tph expression to brain and SEZ (Tph>CsChrimson, tsh>Gal80) eliminated operant conditioning, with no learned direction preference (p>0.05) and significantly lower difference in bend rate (mean=-0.12) compared to Tph>CsChrimson larvae (mean=0.33, p=0.025, CLES=0.58), suggesting VNC serotonergic neurons play a novel role in conveying reward signals for operant conditioning.
results.evaluation: Claims C172-C174 and C192-C193 use intersectional genetics to localize critical neurons to VNC. Statistical comparisons appropriate. The conclusion about VNC serotonergic neurons (C193) is well-supported by the data. This is a novel finding that contrasts with classical conditioning circuits. Sample sizes adequate (n=76 before, n=111 after).

results.result: The authors determined that thermogenetic stimulation is too slow for operant conditioning because average bend duration is 1.35s (sd=1.67s, n=4622) while heating requires ~4s, and increasing laser intensity risks tissue damage. Mild heat is more aversive than red light based on control bending behavior, leading to choice of optogenetics for operant paradigm.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C121 present logical reasoning for methodological choices based on measured parameters. The bend duration measurement (C117) is from substantial data (n=4622). The inference about temporal mismatch (C118) is sound. The comparison of aversiveness (C121) is based on control data from Figures 2D and 2E. This reasoning appropriately guides experimental design.

results.result: The authors did not observe increased attraction to Or42b after backward-paired training, potentially due to slow cooling dynamics causing Basin neurons to remain partially active during subsequent Or42b stimulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C185-C186 acknowledge a negative result and offer speculation (C186). The explanation about residual heat is plausible given measured cooling dynamics (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) but remains untested. This represents an appropriate acknowledgment of limitations and suggests future experiments with optogenetic US for backward-paired training.

results.result: The Drosophila larva is a tractable model system for studying circuit basis of behavior due to powerful genetic tools, uniquely identifiable neurons with preserved morphology/function, binary expression systems, and complete EM-based wiring diagram of the mushroom body, though many forms of associative learning have not yet been demonstrated.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2 and C16-C26 present established knowledge about Drosophila larvae as a model system, supported by extensive citations. These claims provide appropriate context for the study. The statement about many forms of learning not being demonstrated (C2) motivates the current work.

results.result: There is overwhelming evidence that Drosophila larvae are capable of classical conditioning with various CS-US pairings (odor-reward, odor-light, odor-shock, odor-heat, odor-vibration, odor-quinine), and adult flies can perform trace conditioning, but trace conditioning has never been shown in larvae prior to this study.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C37 summarize prior literature with appropriate citations. The statement about absence of larval trace conditioning (C37) reflects the state of knowledge and motivates the current experiments. This provides important context for evaluating the novelty of the trace conditioning result.

results.result: The absence of evidence for trace conditioning in larvae might reflect limitations of current methods rather than genuine learning limitations. Current methods often lack temporal precision, using optogenetic US with natural odor CS, and prior thermogenetic approaches (e.g., hot plates) are slow relative to optogenetics.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C42 present reasonable speculation (C38) about methodological limitations, supported by citations to current approaches (C39, C41). The inference about temporal precision limitations (C40, C42) is logical and motivates the technical development. This reasoning appropriately frames the contribution of the new system.

results.result: Operant conditioning has been demonstrated across vertebrates and invertebrates, but it is unknown whether Drosophila larvae can associate their own actions with sensory outcomes. For such learning, behavioral information must converge with circuits encoding outcome valence, exemplified by vertebrate basal ganglia, though some action-outcome associations do not require the brain.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C48 provide appropriate background on operant conditioning with extensive citations. The statement about unknown capacity in larvae (C45) motivates the study. The theoretical framework about convergence requirements (C46-C48) is well-established and provides context for circuit dissection experiments.

results.result: Prior work in adult flies shows conflicting results about MB involvement in operant conditioning, with some studies suggesting involvement and others suggesting it is not required and may involve motor neuron plasticity. In classical conditioning, the MB is a convergence site for CS and US, comprising ~110 Kenyon cells synapsing onto 24 MBONs, with dopaminergic/octopaminergic modulation. The extent to which MB is dispensable in larval operant conditioning is unknown.
results.evaluation: Claims C138-C144 appropriately summarize conflicting literature on MB involvement in operant conditioning with citations, contrasting with established role in classical conditioning. This provides important context for the negative results with MB-specific drivers (58E02) and motivates circuit dissection experiments.

results.result: Biogenic amine neurotransmitters (dopamine, octopamine, serotonin) can provide reinforcement signals across the animal kingdom. The Ddc-Gal4 driver covers a broad set of dopaminergic and serotonergic neurons including MB-innervating PAM cluster neurons. PAM activation is necessary and sufficient for reward in classical conditioning, and collective Ddc activation can substitute for olfactory reward in adult flies.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C116 provide appropriate background on reward signaling with citations. This establishes the rationale for using Ddc-Gal4 as a starting point for operant conditioning experiments, though the broad expression pattern necessitates subsequent circuit dissection.

results.result: There is growing evidence from classical conditioning that larvae can learn that an unpaired stimulus predicts absence of reinforcement. The authors speculate that larvae may form memories of opposite valence in operant conditioning, bending less to the unstimulated side because it predicts absence of appetitive Ddc activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C136-C137 connect to prior work on inhibitory learning (C136, with citations) and offer speculation about mechanism (C137). The speculation is reasonable given the data pattern (C133-C135) but remains untested. This represents appropriate hypothesis generation for future work.

results.result: Prior work used optogenetic activation of sugar-sensing neurons for operant conditioning in adult flies. The authors were unsuccessful using similar US for larval bend direction conditioning, but suggest other sensory rewards may mediate operant conditioning if information retrieval occurs within the VNC.
results.evaluation: Claims C194-C196 acknowledge a negative result (C195, data not shown) and offer speculation (C196) based on the Ddc and Tph results. The speculation is reasonable but untested. The negative result with sugar-sensing neurons is mentioned but not detailed, limiting evaluation.

results.result: The authors suggest future directions including investigating FoxP and PKC expression (involved in adult operant learning), replicating paradigms with natural stimuli using microfluidic devices, and addressing challenges of low-frequency behaviors through probabilistic thermogenetic activation of command neurons with optogenetic reward.
results.evaluation: Claims C197-C202 present suggestions for future work. These are reasonable directions based on the current findings and prior literature (C198 with citations), but represent speculation about untested approaches. The acknowledgment of validation needs (C199) is appropriate.

results.result: The authors acknowledge a notable limitation: inability to maintain object identity following larval collisions, which could be addressed in future software modifications. The system will enable rapid screening for learning circuits and has potential for studying larval taxis, decision-making, and spatial navigation/memory.
results.evaluation: Claims C204-C207 appropriately acknowledge a technical limitation (C204) and suggest future improvements (C205). The statements about utility (C206-C207) are reasonable inferences based on demonstrated capabilities, though some applications remain to be demonstrated. The acknowledgment of limitations is scientifically appropriate.
